sponsor: Rep. Ro Khanna, with Rep. Thomas Massie

cls.banner: This is binding law. It orders the Attorney General to publish Justice Department records about Jeffrey Epstein within 30 days.
cls.checks: All families run. Definitions, enforcement and scope of who is bound come first for a freestanding mandate.

stated.t: To require the Attorney General to release all documents and records in possession of the Department of Justice relating to Jeffrey Epstein, and for other purposes.

marketed.t: Records cannot be held back on the basis of embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity.
marketed.l: CP24 summary of the bill text

marketed.t: The Attorney General told reporters the Department would follow the law with maximum transparency while protecting victims.

ladder.mechanism: Order one official to publish one department's unclassified records within 30 days.
ladder.outcome: The public can read the government's records on Epstein and the people connected to him.
ladder.aim: Accountability for those involved and for the government's own handling of the case, without further harm to survivors.

promises.p: Release all documents and records relating to Jeffrey Epstein
promises.why: The operative text reaches only unclassified records in the possession of the Department of Justice. Records at other agencies and classified records are outside the mandate.
The deadline is stated, but the Act attaches no consequence to missing it and has no enforcement clause of its own. The deadline passed with about half the pages unreleased.

promises.p: No withholding for embarrassment, reputational harm or political sensitivity
promises.why: The prohibition is clear, but the five permitted grounds in subsection (c) are judged by the same official, and the Act builds in no outside review. A court began reviewing withheld documents only in July 2026, in a suit brought under a different statute.
Redaction of victims' identifying information is permitted, not required.

promises.p: Name the government officials and politically exposed persons in the files
promises.why: The list is due only after the release is complete, goes to two committees and not the public, and uses a term the Act does not define.

questions.q: Section 2(a) says the Attorney General "shall" publish. Where does the Act switch to "may", and what does each "may" leave to that official's choice?
questions.a: One place carries most of the weight: section 2(c)(1), where the Attorney General "may withhold or redact" five categories. The first category is victims' identifying information. Release is commanded; protecting victims is optional.

questions.q: Which words narrow "all documents and records", and what sits on the other side of each word?
questions.a: Two limiters do the narrowing. "Unclassified" excludes anything the executive branch has classified, and the executive controls classification. "In the possession of the Department of Justice" excludes records held anywhere else.

questions.q: Who else in government would hold records about this person?
questions.a: A financier with international travel, a federal prosecution and a death in federal custody leaves records well beyond one department: Treasury and its financial crimes bureau, the IRS, customs and immigration agencies, the State Department, intelligence agencies, the Bureau of Prisons (inside Justice) and the National Archives. Only Justice is named.

s.l: Draft Title VII, listing additional sources

questions.q: If the Attorney General publishes nothing by day 30, what happens next, and who can make it happen?
questions.a: The Act provides nothing. Its sponsors asked one court to appoint a monitor and were told the Act gives the court no such authority. A journalist later obtained an injunction under the Administrative Procedure Act, more than six months after the deadline.

s.l: United States v. Maxwell, opinion of January 21, 2026
Account of the June 2026 injunction

questions.q: Who is affected if this works exactly as written, including the people it is meant to protect?
questions.a: Survivors. A statute that mandates publication at speed and makes redaction of their information optional exposes them to the errors of a rushed review. Survivors and their lawyers reported names appearing in released files and asked the Department's inspector general to step in.

s.l: Survivors on failure to redact victim identities
Survivors urge DOJ watchdog review

questions.q: For an official who preferred to release less, what is the cheapest lawful path?
questions.a: Three are open on the face of the text: classify or keep classified; open or point to an active investigation, since the Act lets that official decide what would "jeopardize" one; or use the broad category for images of death, abuse or injury "of any person".

s.l: How one major exception could allow withholding

questions.q: How did the closest earlier records law handle the same problems?
questions.a: The 1992 law on Kennedy assassination records reached records across the federal government and created an independent review board to decide postponements. This Act has neither feature.

s.l: National Archives: JFK Assassination Records background

questions.q: Do the Act's internal references point where they need to?
questions.a: Two do not. Section 2(a) is made "subject to subsection (b)", the prohibited grounds, and never mentions subsection (c), the permitted withholdings. Section 3(3) cites "subsection (b)(1)" although section 3 has no subsections.

questions.q: What starts the clock on the report to Congress?
questions.a: "Completion of the release." If the release is never declared complete, the report is never due.

questions.q: What is the smallest set of changes that would deliver the stated purpose?
questions.a: Make victim redaction mandatory in its own paragraph; extend the mandate to every agency holding responsive records; put withholding decisions in front of someone other than the official making them; and give the deadline a consequence.

a.ctx: The Attorney general may withhold or redact

findings.title: Redaction of victims' identifying information is permitted but not required.
findings.plain: The law orders the files released but only allows, and does not require, the Attorney General to black out victims' names and personal details. One word makes the difference between a duty and a choice.
findings.tech: Section 2(a) uses "shall" for publication. Section 2(c)(1) uses "may" for all five withholding categories, including (A), victims' personally identifiable information. The Department read it the same way, telling a federal court the Act "does not require withholding or redacting of victim information".
findings.use: An official under a 30-day mandate can publish first and redact imperfectly, and a survivor whose information is released has no statutory duty to point to.

s.l: Department of Justice letter, S.D.N.Y.
Survivors on failure to redact

am.label: Minimal: one word
am.instr: Section 2(c)(1) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act (Public Law 119-38) is amended by striking "may" and inserting "shall".

ops.ctx: The Attorney general may withhold or redact

am.cost: Re-testing this fix shows a side effect. The same "may" governs all five categories, so one word would also require withholding everything that touches an active investigation, images of injury and classified material. It protects victims and mandates more secrecy at once.

am.label: Targeted: separate the victim protection
am.instr: Section 2(c) is amended (1) in paragraph (1), by striking subparagraph (A) and redesignating subparagraphs (B) through (E) as subparagraphs (A) through (D); and (2) by inserting before paragraph (1) a new paragraph requiring redaction of victim information.

ops.before: The Attorney general may withhold or redact
ops.w: (1) REQUIRED REDACTION.--The Attorney General shall redact from any record made publicly available under subsection (a) the personally identifiable information of any victim, and shall withhold victims' personal and medical files and similar files the disclosure of which would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy, unless the victim consents in writing to disclosure.

ops.q: (A) contain personally identifiable information of victims or victims' personal and medical files and similar files the disclosure of which would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy;

am.cost: Mandatory redaction slows release and needs staff. It also needs a definition of "victim", which the Act lacks. The consent clause lets survivors who want to be named be named.

inq.q: What happened to survivors' information when the files were released under this wording?

a.q: in the possession of the Department of Justice, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation and United States Attorneys' Offices

findings.title: The disclosure requirement is limited to records in the possession of the Department of Justice.
findings.plain: The law reaches records held by the Justice Department, and the only offices it names, the FBI and the U.S. Attorneys, are parts of that Department. Records about the same people held anywhere else in the government are not covered.
findings.tech: Section 2(a) limits the mandate to records "in the possession of the Department of Justice, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation and United States Attorneys' Offices". The "including" clause lists components of that Department; it does not extend the mandate to other agencies. A record transferred out of the Department, or never held by it, is outside the Act.
findings.use: A record's location decides whether it is published. Material at Treasury, Homeland Security, State or an intelligence agency stays where it is, and material the Department passes to another agency leaves the Act's reach.

s.l: National Archives: the 1992 JFK records law reached records government-wide

am.label: Extend to every agency
am.instr: Section 2(a) is amended by striking "in the possession of the Department of Justice, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation and United States Attorneys' Offices," and inserting "in the possession, custody, or control of any Federal agency (as defined in section 551 of title 5, United States Code), including the Department of Justice, the Department of the Treasury, the Department of State, the Department of Homeland Security, each element of the intelligence community, and the National Archives and Records Administration,".

ops.q: in the possession of the Department of Justice, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation and United States Attorneys' Offices,
ops.w: in the possession, custody, or control of any Federal agency (as defined in section 551 of title 5, United States Code), including the Department of Justice, the Department of the Treasury, the Department of State, the Department of Homeland Security, each element of the intelligence community, and the National Archives and Records Administration,

am.cost: The Attorney General cannot compel other agency heads, so each head needs to be made responsible for that agency's records. Some record types, such as tax returns and suspicious activity reports, are protected by other statutes that would need to be addressed by name.

inq.q: Where else in the federal government are records about Jeffrey Epstein documented or likely to exist, and does the Act reach them?

findings.pat: Limiter word controlled by the regulated party
findings.title: The disclosure requirement applies only to unclassified records, and classification authority rests with the executive branch.
findings.plain: Only unclassified records must be released. The executive branch decides what is classified, so the official ordered to release also has a say over what counts as releasable.
findings.tech: Section 2(a) covers "all unclassified records". Section 2(c)(3) softens this by directing declassification "to the maximum extent possible" and unclassified summaries, and 2(c)(4) requires notice of classification decisions after July 1, 2025. But "maximum extent possible" is a feasibility qualifier judged by the same official, and notice of a new classification does not undo it.
findings.use: Material can be classified, or left classified, and replaced with a summary written by the withholding agency.

s.l: Draft Title VII on congressional declassification

am.label: Require a classified annex to Congress and independent review
am.instr: Section 2(c)(3) is amended by adding at the end the following: "(B) Not later than 30 days after making a determination under subparagraph (A), the Attorney General shall transmit the unredacted covered information to the Select Committee on Intelligence of the Senate and the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence of the House of Representatives, and shall refer the determination to the Public Interest Declassification Board for review."

ops.after: the Attorney General shall release an unclassified summary
ops.w: (B) Not later than 30 days after making a determination under subparagraph (A), the Attorney General shall transmit the unredacted covered information to the Select Committee on Intelligence of the Senate and the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence of the House of Representatives, and shall refer the determination to the Public Interest Declassification Board for review.

am.cost: This adds oversight but not public release. A stronger version, in which Congress itself orders declassification, raises a separation of powers dispute and would be litigated.

two.dec: Should classification decisions affecting these records be subject to review by a court or an independent body?

views.why: One member has asked the CIA to search classified holdings.

s.l: Rep. Mace letter to the CIA

a.q: Not later than 30 days after the date of enactment of this Act

findings.title: The Act sets a 30-day deadline for release and specifies no consequence for missing it.
findings.plain: The law sets a 30-day deadline, but says nothing about what happens if it is missed. No one is given the power to enforce it.
findings.tech: The deadline in 2(a) is not paired with a penalty, a default rule, a reporting trigger or a cause of action anywhere in the Act. Courts are generally reluctant to compel agency action on a statutory timetable without a clear enforcement provision.
findings.use: Release can proceed in batches on the Department's own schedule.

s.l: DOJ missing deadline to publish all files

findings.pat: Cross-reference points to the wrong provision
findings.title: The release requirement is made subject to the subsection listing prohibited grounds, not the subsection listing permitted withholdings.
findings.plain: The release requirement says it is "subject to subsection (b)". Subsection (b) lists reasons that cannot be used to withhold. The reasons that can be used are in subsection (c), which the release requirement never mentions.
findings.tech: As enacted, 2(a) is "subject to subsection (b)" (prohibited grounds). The permitted withholdings are in 2(c). A Senate companion text made the release duty subject to its permitted-withholdings subsection, which suggests the reference was not updated when subsections were reordered. Read literally, the relationship between the "shall" in (a) and the "may" in (c) is left to inference.
findings.use: Either side can argue from the gap: that (c) does not qualify (a) at all, or that (c) is a free-standing discretion not bounded by (a).

s.l: Senate companion text, S. 2557

am.label: Correct the reference
am.instr: Section 2(a) is amended by striking "subject to subsection (b)" and inserting "subject to subsections (b) and (c)".
am.cost: None beyond confirming the intended reading.

findings.title: The reporting section cites a subsection that does not exist in the Act.
findings.plain: Section 3 points to "subsection (b)(1)", but section 3 has no subsections. It almost certainly means section 2(b)(1).
findings.tech: Under ordinary drafting convention an unqualified "subsection (b)(1)" refers to the section in which it appears. Section 3 has paragraphs (1) through (3) only. The phrase "no redactions permitted under subsection (b)(1)" is also ambiguous: 2(b)(1) prohibits grounds for withholding; it does not permit redactions.
findings.use: Whether names in the list to Congress can be redacted on the 2(c) grounds is unclear.

am.label: Fix the reference and the meaning
am.instr: Section 3(3) is amended by striking "with no redactions permitted under subsection (b)(1)" and inserting "with no name withheld or redacted on any ground described in section 2(b)(1)".

ops.q: with no redactions permitted under subsection (b)(1)
ops.w: with no name withheld or redacted on any ground described in section 2(b)(1)

findings.title: The Act requires a list of "politically exposed persons" and does not define the term.
findings.plain: The report to Congress must list "politically exposed persons" named in the files. The law does not say who counts.
findings.tech: The term comes from anti-money-laundering practice, where it generally refers to senior foreign officials and their close associates. Without a definition or a cross-reference, the compiler of the list chooses its breadth.
findings.use: A narrow reading shortens the list.

findings.pat: Exception controlled by the regulated party
findings.title: The exception for active investigations has no stated standard, duration or external review.
findings.plain: Records can be held back if release would jeopardize an active investigation, as long as the withholding is "narrowly tailored and temporary". The law does not say how narrow, how long, or who checks.
findings.tech: Section 2(c)(1)(C) conditions the exception on tailoring and temporariness but supplies no time limit, no periodic re-justification and no reviewer. The Department that decides whether an investigation is active is the same Department applying the exception.
findings.use: An open investigation can support withholding for as long as it stays open.

s.l: How one major exception could allow withholding

am.label: Add a clock and a re-justification
am.instr: Section 2(c)(1)(C) is amended by striking "narrowly tailored and temporary" and inserting "narrowly tailored, expires not later than 180 days after it begins unless the Attorney General certifies in writing to the Committees on the Judiciary of the House of Representatives and the Senate the specific investigation or prosecution that continued withholding would jeopardize, and is renewed only by a new certification every 180 days".

ops.w: narrowly tailored, expires not later than 180 days after it begins unless the Attorney General certifies in writing to the Committees on the Judiciary of the House of Representatives and the Senate the specific investigation or prosecution that continued withholding would jeopardize, and is renewed only by a new certification every 180 days

am.cost: Certifications can become routine. The 180-day figure is a policy choice.

a.q: depict or contain images of death, physical abuse, or injury of any person

findings.title: The exception for images of death, abuse or injury extends to any record that contains such an image.
findings.plain: Any record that depicts or contains images of death, abuse or injury "of any person" may be withheld or redacted. That protects dignity, and it also reaches a large amount of evidence.
findings.tech: Section 2(c)(1)(D) is not limited to victims or to images whose release would be an invasion of privacy. Because (c)(1) speaks of "segregable portions", the better reading confines withholding to the images themselves, but "contain" invites withholding of the surrounding record.
findings.use: Reports that include a photograph can be treated as withholdable records.

a.q: Within 15 days of completion of the release

findings.title: The reporting deadline runs from completion of the release, which the Act does not require anyone to certify.
findings.plain: The Attorney General must report to Congress within 15 days of finishing the release. If the release is never declared finished, the report is never due.
findings.tech: Section 3 keys the reporting duty to "completion of the release required under Section 2" and not to the 30-day deadline. A rolling release has no completion date unless the Department announces one. The report also goes to two committees, with no requirement that it be public.
findings.use: The list of categories withheld, the legal basis for redactions and the list of named officials can be deferred indefinitely.

am.label: Tie the report to a date
am.instr: Section 3 is amended by striking "Within 15 days of completion of the release required under Section 2" and inserting "Not later than 45 days after the date of enactment of this Act, and every 30 days thereafter until the release required under section 2 is complete", and by adding at the end: "Each report under this section shall be made publicly available."

ops.q: Within 15 days of completion of the release required under Section 2
ops.w: Not later than 45 days after the date of enactment of this Act, and every 30 days thereafter until the release required under section 2 is complete

am.cost: Recurring reports add workload. Publication of the named-persons list raises reputational questions for people named but not accused.

findings.pat: Justification duty narrower than the discretion

a.q: All redactions must be accompanied by a written justification

findings.title: Published justifications are required for redactions but not for records withheld in full.
findings.plain: Redactions need a written justification published in the Federal Register. The law lets records be withheld or redacted, but the justification rule mentions only redactions and sets no deadline.
findings.tech: Section 2(c)(1) permits the Attorney General to "withhold or redact". Section 2(c)(2) requires justification for "redactions" only, uses "must" where the rest of the Act uses "shall", and gives no timing or level of detail.
findings.use: A record withheld entirely arguably needs no published justification.

am.label: Cover withholdings and set timing
am.instr: Section 2(c)(2) is amended by striking "All redactions must be accompanied by a written justification" and inserting "Each withholding and each redaction shall be accompanied, at the time of release, by a written justification identifying the specific subparagraph of paragraph (1) relied upon, and such justification shall be".

ops.q: All redactions must be accompanied by a written justification
ops.w: Each withholding and each redaction shall be accompanied, at the time of release, by a written justification identifying the specific subparagraph of paragraph (1) relied upon, and such justification shall be

am.cost: Per-item justifications for millions of pages are costly; category-level justifications may be the workable form.

findings.title: The Attorney General's title is capitalized inconsistently in one provision.
findings.plain: "Attorney general" appears once with a lowercase g. It does not change the meaning, but it is a sign the text was not proofread against itself before passage.
findings.tech: The officer is "Attorney General" everywhere else in the Act. Harmless, and the kind of error the enrolled text carries forward permanently.

am.label: Correct the capitalization
am.instr: Section 2(c)(1) is amended by striking "Attorney general" and inserting "Attorney General".

findings.pat: No enforcement mechanism in the statute
findings.title: The Act contains no penalty, no judicial review provision and no private right of action.
findings.plain: The Act contains no penalty, no court review and no stated right to sue. When the deadline passed, its own sponsors were turned away by one court. A different court later allowed a journalist's suit under a general law, six months after the deadline.
findings.tech: There is no cause of action, no grant of jurisdiction, no inspector general role and no consequence for noncompliance in the text. Enforcement has depended on finding a general statute that fits and a plaintiff with standing. A later bill, H.R. 9694, would add enforcement by state attorneys general and by victims.
findings.use: Each attempt to enforce starts with a fight over whether any court can hear it. That fight consumed the months in which the release was supposed to happen.

s.l: H.R. 9694, Epstein Files Transparency Act II

am.label: Add judicial enforcement
am.instr: The Act is amended by adding at the end the following: "SEC. 4. ENFORCEMENT. (a) Any person may bring a civil action in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia to compel compliance with section 2 or 3. (b) The court shall examine withheld or redacted material in camera and shall determine de novo whether each withholding is authorized by section 2(c). (c) The court may award reasonable attorney fees and costs to a plaintiff who substantially prevails."

ops.w:
SEC. 4. ENFORCEMENT.
(a) Any person may bring a civil action in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia to compel compliance with section 2 or 3.
(b) The court shall examine withheld or redacted material in camera and shall determine de novo whether each withholding is authorized by section 2(c).
(c) The court may award reasonable attorney fees and costs to a plaintiff who substantially prevails.

am.cost: "Any person" standing invites a constitutional standing challenge; H.R. 9694 takes a narrower route through state attorneys general and victims. Litigation takes time the 30-day design did not contemplate.

inq.q: What happened when people tried to enforce the Act?

items.d: Reps. Massie and Khanna asked the judge in the Maxwell criminal case to appoint a special master to oversee compliance, citing the missed December 19, 2025 deadline, a report that was never filed and excessive redactions. On January 21, 2026 Judge Engelmayer denied the request, writing that the Act is a civil records statute and no provision of it gives the court that authority.

s.l: United States v. Maxwell, opinion of January 21, 2026

items.h: A journalist got further under a general statute
items.d: Katie Phang sued under the Administrative Procedure Act in the federal court in Washington. The government argued the Freedom of Information Act was the only remedy. Judge Sullivan rejected that, found she had standing because she was denied information, and in late June 2026 ordered specific redactions lifted and redaction logs published.

s.l: Account of the June 2026 injunction

items.h: Court review of withheld documents began in July 2026
items.d: On July 25, 2026 the judge ordered the Department to hand over disputed documents for private review. The plaintiff asked for a fine of $1,000 a day. An appeal was expected.

s.l: Forbes, July 27, 2026

items.h: Redactions are being audited after the fact
items.d: The Government Accountability Office is reviewing the redactions at the request of members of Congress. The Act did not require that review.

s.l: CBS News: what is missing from the Epstein files

inq.open: Whether the Administrative Procedure Act route survives appeal is not settled. If it does not, the Act returns to having no judicial enforcement.

findings.pat: The current holder has a tie to an affected person
findings.title: The Epstein Files Transparency Act assigns release and withholding decisions to the Attorney General, and both Attorneys General since enactment previously served as lawyers for President Trump.
findings.plain: Sections 2 and 3 of the Epstein Files Transparency Act give the Attorney General the duty to release the Epstein records, the discretion to withhold them and the duty to report on what was withheld. Both people who have held that office since enactment previously served as lawyers for President Trump: Pam Bondi until April 2026, and Todd Blanche since then. News reports state that Pam Bondi told the President in May 2025 that his name appeared in the Epstein files, at a briefing that Todd Blanche attended. The Act has no recusal rule and names no other decision-maker.
findings.tech: The President appoints the Attorney General and may remove that official, and he removed Pam Bondi in April 2026. The reports of the May 2025 briefing say the significance of the references to the President is not clear, and the Department of Justice said that nothing in the files warranted further investigation. A separate, structural conflict exists whoever holds the office, because section 2(a) of the Act covers the Department's own internal communications about decisions to charge or not charge Epstein. Congress has addressed comparable conflicts before, through the independent counsel provisions of the Ethics in Government Act of 1978, which lapsed in 1999, and through the independent review board in the 1992 Kennedy records law.
findings.use: An Attorney General who previously represented the President can apply the withholding categories in section 2(c) of the Act to Epstein records that concern the President, and no independent body is positioned to test those decisions.

s.l: Star Tribune (New York Times report), July 2025
Fortune, November 22, 2024
The Week, August 10, 2026
Congressional Research Service, Special Counsel Investigations (R44857)

items.h: The 1992 law on Kennedy assassination records gave decisions about postponing release to an independent review board.
items.d: Congress did not leave those decisions to the agencies that held the Kennedy assassination records. The Epstein Files Transparency Act has no comparable board.

s.l: National Archives: JFK Assassination Records background

inq.open: It is not publicly known which Epstein records the Department of Justice withheld because they concern the President or the Department's own conduct.

am.label: Outside decision-maker for records about the Department or the President
am.instr: Section 2 of the Epstein Files Transparency Act (Public Law 119-38) is amended by adding at the end the following: "(d) Independent Determination.--Any determination under subsection (c) to withhold or redact a record that refers to the President, the Vice President, the Attorney General, or the conduct of an officer or employee of the Department of Justice shall be made by the Inspector General of the Department of Justice, who shall provide any written justification that this section requires.".

ops.w: (d) Independent Determination.--Any determination under subsection (c) to withhold or redact a record that refers to the President, the Vice President, the Attorney General, or the conduct of an officer or employee of the Department of Justice shall be made by the Inspector General of the Department of Justice, who shall provide any written justification that this section requires.

am.cost: Moving these determinations to the Inspector General of the Department of Justice adds a reviewer outside the chain of command for the release, at a cost in speed. The President appoints the Inspector General and may remove that official after 30 days' notice to Congress, so this option reduces the conflict without removing it. A review board modeled on the 1992 Kennedy records law would be more independent and would take longer to establish.

findings.title: The Act does not define "victim", "associate" or "related entity".
findings.plain: The Act has no definitions. It does not say who is a "victim", who counts as one of Epstein's "associates", or what a "related entity" is.
findings.tech: "Victims" controls the reach of the privacy protection in 2(c)(1)(A). "Associates" controls the scope of categories (6), (7) and (8) in 2(a). Neither is defined or cross-referenced to an existing statutory definition.
findings.use: A narrow reading of "victim" exposes people who were never formally identified as victims in a charging document. A narrow reading of "associates" shrinks the release.

am.label: Add a definition of victim
am.instr: The Act is amended by inserting after section 1 the following: "SEC. 1A. DEFINITIONS. In this Act, the term 'victim' means any individual who was, or who is described in a covered record as having been, subjected to sexual abuse, trafficking, or exploitation by Jeffrey Epstein or any associate of Jeffrey Epstein, whether or not the individual was identified in any charging document, and includes any individual who was a minor at the time of the events described."

ops.before: SEC. 2. RELEASE OF DOCUMENTS RELATING TO JEFFREY EPSTEIN.
ops.w:
SEC. 1A. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act, the term "victim" means any individual who was, or who is described in a covered record as having been, subjected to sexual abuse, trafficking, or exploitation by Jeffrey Epstein or any associate of Jeffrey Epstein, whether or not the individual was identified in any charging document, and includes any individual who was a minor at the time of the events described.

am.cost: A broad definition increases redaction work and could be used to shield names of adults who were participants; the drafting has to separate the two.

two.dec: Which official applies the undefined terms, and does that official have an incentive to construe them narrowly?

views.why: An undefined term leaves the Department to decide who counts. It has cited victim status as a reason for redactions.

s.l: Forbes, July 27, 2026

findings.pat: The regulated official is the only decision-maker
findings.title: Withholding decisions are made and reported by the Attorney General without independent review.
findings.plain: The Attorney General decides what to withhold, writes the justification and reports on it. No one outside the Department checks those decisions.
findings.tech: Compare the 1992 Kennedy records law, which placed postponement decisions with an independent review board. Here the prohibited-grounds rule in 2(b)(1) depends on the good faith of the official who might be embarrassed.
findings.use: A withholding made for a prohibited reason can be labeled with a permitted one.

conflicts.who: Todd Blanche, Attorney General since April 2026
conflicts.claim: Attorney General Todd Blanche, who now holds the authority to withhold Epstein records, is President Trump's former personal lawyer.
conflicts.detail: Todd Blanche was Deputy Attorney General when the Epstein Files Transparency Act took effect. He became acting Attorney General in April 2026 and was confirmed by the Senate, 50 to 49, in August 2026. News reports describe him as the President's former personal lawyer and close ally. News reports also state that he attended the May 2025 briefing at which the President was told that his name appeared in the Epstein files. Those reports say the significance of the references is not clear. The Act contains no recusal rule for an official with such a tie.

s.l: The Week, August 10, 2026
Star Tribune (New York Times report), July 2025

conflicts.who: Pam Bondi, Attorney General until April 2026
conflicts.claim: Pam Bondi, who was Attorney General when the Act took effect and during the first releases of Epstein records, had previously served as a lawyer for President Trump.
conflicts.detail: Pam Bondi joined President Trump's legal team during his first impeachment trial in 2020. News reports state that she told the President in May 2025 that his name appeared in the Epstein files, and that she and her deputy said nothing in the files warranted further investigation or prosecution. The President removed her as Attorney General in April 2026.

s.l: Fortune, November 22, 2024

conflicts.detail: The Epstein Files Transparency Act gives the Attorney General sole authority over the release and withholding of Epstein records. The President removed one Attorney General in April 2026 and nominated her successor. The Act has no separate procedure for Epstein records that concern the President.

conflicts.claim: The Department of Justice decides what to release from records that document its own decisions in the Epstein case.
conflicts.detail: Section 2(a) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act covers internal Department communications about decisions to charge or not charge Epstein, non-prosecution agreements and records of his death in federal custody. The Act names no decision-maker outside the Department and requires no outside review of what is withheld.
